nameStory: The Orange-banded Arion gets its name from the distinctive orange or yellowish stripe that runs along each side of its body. This colorful band makes it stand out from its more drably colored slug relatives, acting like racing stripes on nature's slowest racer!
description: The Orange-banded Arion is a completely shell-less land slug that breathes air through a lung-like cavity. Like other roundback slugs, it has a distinctly humped or rounded back when moving, rather than a flat profile. These medium-sized slugs are most notable for their striking orange to yellow lateral bands that contrast with their darker body color. They're part of a large family of European slugs that have established populations in parts of New England.

idTips.label: Orange side bands
idTips.description: Look for bright orange to yellowish stripes running along each side of the body from head to tail - these bands are the slug's signature feature and remain visible even when the animal contracts

idTips.label: Rounded back profile
idTips.description: When active, the back appears distinctly humped or rounded rather than flattened, giving it a more three-dimensional appearance than many other slug species

idTips.label: Breathing pore location
idTips.description: The pneumostome (breathing hole) is located on the right side of the body behind the head - you can sometimes see it opening and closing rhythmically

idTips.label: Mucus trail texture
idTips.description: Leaves a clear, slightly sticky slime trail that feels slippery between your fingers and may have a faint musty smell

idTips.label: Body color variation
idTips.description: The main body color ranges from grayish-brown to darker brown or black, but the orange bands remain consistent and vibrant

habitat: Orange-banded Arions prefer moist, shaded environments like deciduous and mixed forests where they can find shelter under logs, leaf litter, and rocks. They're often found in gardens and landscaped areas with rich, organic soil and plenty of decomposing plant matter. Look for them in areas that stay consistently damp, especially near compost piles or mulched garden beds.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture increases. Look under logs and in leaf litter during mild, damp days when they emerge to feed.
seasonality.summer: Active during cool, humid mornings and after rain showers. During hot, dry periods they retreat deep into soil or under cover and may be harder to find.
seasonality.fall: Very active in the cooler, moister conditions. This is an excellent time to spot them as they feed heavily before winter.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, hiding deep in soil, under logs, or in other protected spots. May occasionally be found during warm winter thaws.

funFact: Despite being one of nature's slowest creatures, slugs like the Orange-banded Arion can actually find their way home using their own slime trails like a GPS system - they can follow their mucus back to their favorite hiding spots even after traveling surprisingly long distances for such small animals!
confusionNotes: The orange side bands make this species fairly distinctive, but young individuals or faded specimens might be confused with other Arion slugs. Remember the key difference: if you see those orange racing stripes, you've found your Orange-banded Arion - no other local slug species has such prominent colored side bands.
contextualKnowledge: This species, like many Arion slugs, is originally from Europe and was likely introduced to North America accidentally through plant commerce or soil transport. The scientific name 'fasciatus' literally means 'banded,' referring to those distinctive orange stripes that make identification possible.
compareHints: Among its Arion relatives in New England, the Orange-banded Arion is the only one with prominent orange side bands - the Black Slug is uniformly dark, the Garden Arion is typically smaller and grayer, and the Dusky Slugs lack any bright coloration. Those orange stripes are your dead giveaway that you're looking at A. fasciatus rather than its more subdued cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Arion slugs, the Western Dusky Slug is one of the smallest and plainest-looking members of its genus.
Among its Arion relatives, the hedgehog slug is most distinctive for its defensive curling behavior - the Black Slug and Garden Arion don't ball up nearly as dramatically.
Garden Arions are smaller and more compact than their relatives like the Black Slug, which can grow much larger and stays more elongated when disturbed.

Black Slugs are the largest and most robust of the Arion genus in New England, with that distinctive rounded back that sets them apart from their smaller, more elongated relatives like the Western Dusky Slug or Garden Arion.
Within the Arion genus, the Northern Dusky Slug is much smaller and more subdued in color compared to the large, jet-black Black Slug or the distinctively marked Orange-banded Arion.

Among New England's Arion slugs, the Darkface Arion is most easily distinguished by its characteristic dark facial markings, while the Garden Arion tends to be more uniformly colored and the Black Slug is typically much larger and darker overall.
